sources.title: Path (graph theory)
sources.venue: Wikipedia, English edition, section 'Walk, trail, and path'
sources.notes: Read the raw wikitext of the page (action=raw) on 2026-11-05 and copied the quotes with markup removed. Revision id not recorded. The page cites Bender and Williamson (2010), p. 162, for the trail and path definitions; that book was not read. Used only for the English naming (trail, path, simple path) that Definitions 1.2.12 and 1.2.13 of the textbook are compared with; encyclopedia text, editable, tertiary.

claims.text: In a simple graph a walk is determined by its vertex sequence u_0, u_1, ..., u_k, because the edge u_{i-1}u_i is the only edge between those two vertices. So a walk of length k from n_i to n_j is the same data as a sequence of k+1 vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent. The textbook abbreviates a walk by its vertex sequence in the same way; Grinberg defines a walk for simple graphs as the vertex sequence.

support.quote: ենթադրելով, որ յուրաքանչյուր հաջորդ գագաթ հարևան է նախորդին:
A walk (in G) means a finite sequence (v0 , v1 , . . . , vk ) of vertices of G (with k ≥ 0) such that all of v0 v1 , v1 v2 , v2 v3 , . . . , vk−1 vk are edges of G.

claims.text: Convention of the paper: a walk of length 0 (a single vertex) is allowed, and it is a path, a trail and a closed walk. Grinberg allows k >= 0. The textbook's Definition 1.2.10 does not say whether k = 0 is allowed, and its Lemma 1.2.1 excludes u = v, so this is the paper's choice, made so that 'every walk contains a path' also holds when the ends coincide.

claims.text: English usage (as in Wikipedia and Grinberg): a trail is a walk with all edges distinct; a path is a walk, equivalently a trail, with all vertices distinct. Some authors say 'simple path' for the latter. This matches the textbook's Definition 1.2.12 ('path' = English trail) and Definition 1.2.13 ('simple path' = English path), so the course word 'path' (no repeated vertices) is the English word 'path' and the textbook's own word 'path' is the English 'trail'.

support.quote: A trail is a walk in which all edges are distinct.
A path is a trail in which all vertices (and therefore also all edges) are distinct.
Some authors do not require that all vertices of a path be distinct and instead use the term simple path to refer to such a path where all vertices are distinct.
A path (in G) means a walk (in G) whose vertices are distinct.
G գրաֆի (u0, uk)-ճանապարհը կանվանենք պարզ (u0, uk)-ճանապարհ, եթե նրա մեջ մտնող բոլոր գագաթները զույգ առ զույգ տարբեր են:

claims.text: Every simple path (no repeated vertex) is a trail (no repeated edge), and every trail is a walk; neither inclusion reverses. Proof of the first: if the edge u_{i-1}u_i equalled u_{j-1}u_j with i < j, then u_{i-1} would equal u_{j-1} or u_j, two vertices with larger index, against distinctness. Strictness: on the textbook's graph of Fig. 1.2.5, v1,v3,v2,v4,v3,v5 is a trail with v3 repeated, and v1,v3,v2,v4,v3,v2,v4,v3,v5 is a walk that is not a trail. Grinberg leaves the first inclusion as Exercise 2.9.

support.quote: Նկատենք, որ նկ. 1.2.5-ի G գրաֆի v1, v3, v2, v4, v3, v5 շրջանցումը ճանապարհ է, իսկ v1, v3, v2, v4, v3, v2, v4, v3, v5-ը՝ ոչ:
Let G be a simple graph. Let w be a path in G. Prove that the edges of w are distinct.

claims.text: Lemma (walk to path, with length bound): in a simple graph, if there is a walk of length k from u to v (u = v allowed), there is a path from u to v of length at most k, formed by some of the walk's vertices in their order. Proof by strong induction on k: if no vertex repeats the walk is a path; otherwise cut out the part between two equal vertices u_i = u_j (i < j), which leaves a walk from u to v of length k - (j - i) < k. The textbook's Lemma 1.2.1 states the case u different from v by induction on the length, without the bound; Grinberg's Proposition 2.9.5 and Corollary 2.9.7 give the shortening and the bound.

support.quote: Ապացույցը կատարենք մակածման եղանակով ըստ (u, v)-շրջանցման k երկարության:
Assume that a is not a path. Then, there exists a walk from u to v whose length is smaller than k.
Assume that there is a walk from u to v of length k for some k ∈ N. Then, there is a path from u to v of length ≤ k.

claims.text: For two vertices u and v of a simple graph the following are equivalent: a walk from u to v exists; a trail from u to v exists; a simple path from u to v exists. Proof: path implies trail (M2-4), trail implies walk (definition), walk implies path (M2-6). Hence the textbook's Definition 2.1.1 (whose 'path' is the 1.2.12 trail), the board's definition and the reading with simple paths define the same connected graphs. Grinberg states the walk-path equivalence only (Proposition 2.9.10) and says nothing about trails, so the trail part is the paper's own.

support.quote: G գրաֆը կանվանենք կապակցված, եթե նրա ցանկացած երկու u և v գագաթների համար G գրաֆում գոյություն ունի (u, v)-ճանապարհ:
Then, u ≃G v if and only if there exists a path from u to v.

claims.text: Distance, Definition 1.2.16, does not depend on which of the three readings is used: the length of a shortest walk, shortest trail and shortest path between u and v are equal when one exists (a shortest walk is a path by M2-6, and a path is a trail and a walk), so d(u,v) = +infinity exactly when no walk exists. When finite, d(u,v) <= N - 1 because a path of length k has k + 1 distinct vertices. The textbook lists three distance axioms; Grinberg notes that a shortest walk is a shortest path.

support.quote: կսահմանենք որպես կարճագույն (u, v)-ճանապարհի երկարություն, եթե G գրաֆում գոյություն ունի առնվազն մեկ (u, v)-ճանապարհ, և +∞՝ հակառակ դեպքում:
G գրաֆի ցանկացած u, v և w գագաթների համար dG(u, v) ≤ dG(u, w) + dG(w, v):
a shortest walk from u to v (if it exists) must also be a shortest path from u to v

claims.derivation: modules/m2.md, section 5, Proposition 2.5; modules/m2_checks.py parts 4 and 5

claims.text: In the textbook a cycle (Definition 1.2.14) is a closed trail, and a simple cycle (1.2.15) repeats only its first and last vertex. In a simple graph (no loops, no multiple edges) a simple cycle has length at least 3: length 1 needs a loop, and length 2 would use the same edge twice, against distinct edges. The textbook writes the simple cycle on n vertices as C_n with n >= 3. Note the book's Definition 1.2.14 is about its 'path', so a cycle there is a closed trail, not a closed simple path.

claims.text: Course convention for 'path between n_i and n_j': a simple (n_i, n_j)-path of textbook Definition 1.2.13, that is a walk n_i = w_0, ..., w_k = n_j with pairwise distinct vertices. For i = j the only such path is the length-0 path. The board's definition of connected says 'a path between nodes'; the user stated that path means no repeated vertices, and that statement is recorded in the brief, not in a source file, so this reading of the board's word is an assumption.

support.quote: G գրաֆի (u0, uk)-ճանապարհը կանվանենք պարզ (u0, uk)-ճանապարհ, եթե նրա մեջ մտնող բոլոր գագաթները զույգ առ զույգ տարբեր են:
Def. Graph is called connected if for any n_i, n_j (exists) path between nodes
